newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's party fail to agree dual nationality plan.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's party fail to agree dual nationality plan.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats failed to agree on Monday on a plan which would have offered German nationality to the children of immigrants.
The proposal would have conceded for the first time that German nationality is not just a matter of blood lines and can be acquired by being born in Germany.

Young members of Kohl's CDU have attracted a great deal of attention with plans to give dual nationality to immigrants' children born in Germany, but make them choose at maturity between German citizenship and that of their parents' country.
Germany is currently the only major Western industrial nation to maintain the principle, enshrined in an Imperial law of 1913, that nationality is essentially passed down from parents.
But the taboo-breaking plan hit stubborn opposition from older CDU members and above all from the arch-conservative Christian Social Union, the Christian Democrats' Bavarian sister party.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze told reporters no decision was made and no timetable set, after the leadership had agreed only that "better integration of foreigners should not be reduced to the issue of dual nationality".
Advocates of reform lobbied hard before the meeting, saying action was needed to stop young immigrants becoming resentful and drifting into ghettos or turning to extremist groups.

"If I am born in Germany, go to school here, train for a job here... then I have automatically become German," Horst Eylmann of the CDU, chairman of parliament's interior affairs committee, told North German Radio.

But Interior Minister Manfred Kanther heads the chorus of those within the party who, along with the Bavarian conservatives, say German nationality should not be a means to integration, but a reward for it.

"What difference does a passport make to the fact that a child of immigrants can feel foreign here because it has a different religion, skin of a different colour, speaks poor German or is treated badly by unpleasant contemporaries?" Kanther asked in an interview earlier this month.
Most of Germany's seven million foreigners are "guest workers" from Turkey, Yugoslavia and other countries who began coming in the 1960s to help fuel a post-war economic boom.
Around a quarter of them were born in Germany. They speak perfect German and feel Germany is their home, yet are excluded from the vote and from a large number of public sector jobs.
By contrast, more than 1.5 million ethnic Germans who have come here from eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union in the last eight years face no such restrictions.
